text: 11 1 Summary • The global extreme poverty rate fell steadily for three decades, from 43 percent in 1990 to 11 percent in 2020. This was an incredible accomplishment. However, progress has since come to a standstill. The extreme poverty rate has remained essentially unchanged after an increase during the COVID pandemic and the subsequent recovery. In 2026, 811 million people—1 in 10 globally—were living in extreme poverty, defined as living on less than $3.00-a-person-a-day in 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP) terms. • Extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated. More than half the extreme poor globally are living in only nine economies, and three-quarters in 20 economies. Of the nine economies, six are in Sub-Saharan Africa, where the extreme poverty rate has remained near 44 percent since 2014. Only in 2026 did poverty rates in Sub-Saharan Africa return to prepandemic levels, while

text: this is still not the case in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan (MENAAP) region. • Fragility is the defining feature of global poverty. The share of the extreme poor living in a fragile and conflict-affected situation (FCS) rose from 12 percent in 2010 to 57 percent in 2026, as more high-poverty economies became fragile and because extreme poverty fell more quickly in non-FCS economies. By 2030, 87 percent of the extreme poor globally will be living in Sub-Saharan Africa or in an FCS economy or both. • If the per capita economic growth rates observed over 2015–24 persist, the global extreme poverty rate and the number of people living in extreme poverty will increase by 2030: an unprecedented reversal of the decades-long decline. Population growth in high-poverty economies is a key factor in the potential increase.

text: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades Following the decades during which global extreme poverty fell at historic rates, the decline has come to a dramatic stop.1 Extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated in economies in Sub-Saharan Africa and in economies experiencing fragility, conflict, and violence. In these economies, poverty rates have generally stagnated or risen. Population growth in these economies, combined with rates of poverty reduction that are insufficient to sustain the progress achieved during the preceding years, means that the number of people living in extreme poverty globally is projected to increase in coming decades.

text: After decades of progress, the reduction in extreme poverty has ground to a halt After decades of significant and steady progress, the reduction of global poverty has reached a critical juncture. In 1990, nearly 2.3 billion people—43 percent of the global population—were living in extreme poverty, defined as living on less than $3.00-a-person-a-day (in 2021 PPP terms) (refer to box 1.1). By 2019, the number had fallen dramatically, to 837 million people, or 10.8 percent of the global population. But, since then, virtually no progress on reducing extreme poverty has been made. The COVID-19 pandemic triggered the largest setback in decades (Mahler et al. 2022). In 2026, 811 million people—1 in 10 globally—were living in extreme poverty, and this rate has remained essentially unchanged since 2020. Factoring in the economic growth and price impacts of the conflict in the Middle East suggests

In June 2025, the base year for comparing price levels across economies was updated from 2017 to 2021 (Alfani et al. 2025). PPPs are used to convert welfare data and national poverty lines from local currency units into dollars. a As part of the update, the global poverty lines were revised to reflect updated national poverty lines set by national authorities around the world. The World Bank’s global poverty lines are based on the national poverty lines that are used by governments to monitor poverty within national borders. The international poverty line is the median national poverty

It thus reflects the typical standard by which governments in the poorest economies define poverty at the national level. Upward revisions in national poverty lines, especially in West Africa, have stemmed from improvements in household survey methodologies that have resulted in higher measured consumption and thus also upward revisions in national poverty lines. These higher national poverty lines do not reflect a more generous standard of what it means to be poor. They reflect better data to assess the cost of basic needs for a minimum food bundle and an allowance for essential nonfood consumption.

text: BOX 1.2 Tracking the impact on poverty of the conflict in the Middle East The conflict in the Middle East and the associated increase in energy prices impacted projected economic growth in 2026. Nearly two in three countries were facing weaker growth prospects in June 2026 compared with the outlook in Global Economic Prospects, January 2026 (World Bank 2026b, 2026c). According to the projections of Global Economic Prospects, June 2026 (World Bank 2026c), commodity prices were expected to rise by 22 percent in 2026, while, according to earlier projections in January 2026, they had been expected to decline by 7 percent in 2026 (World Bank 2026b). The higher commodity prices led to a resurgence of inflationary pressures similar to the situation observed at the start of the Russian Federation’s invasion of Ukraine, which resulted in a reduction in food production, particularly of wheat. What

text: was different this time was that the shock has primarily affected energy prices, and these exert an impact on household budgets directly, but also indirectly through, for example, higher transport costs for food. Furthermore, there has been a significant rise in fertilizer prices, which has affected food production throughout 2026. More generally, energy intensity varies by economic sectors. So, household income can be affected differentially depending on the sector of employment.

Record maize harvests in South Africa (Crop Estimates Committee 2026) fixed fertilizer prices in some countries, such as India (PIB 2026), and the low take-up of fertilizers in Sub-Saharan Africa (FAO 2025) generally could mitigate the impact on food prices. Furthermore, the overall effect of higher food prices on extreme poverty is complicated by the fact that many of the poor are food producers and could thus benefit from higher food prices (Ivanic and Martin 2008). It is thus crucial to understand what happens to input costs. text: 15 Global Poverty: Stalled Pro GreSS and riSinG Con Centration The 2026 nowcasts for poverty presented throughout this report use the growth rates in real per capita gross domestic product (GDP) of Global Economic Prospects, June 2026 (World Bank 2026c).a The baseline estimates assume that the incomes of everyone in the country grow at the same rate. However, higher prices for food and energy will affect households to a varying degree. Typically, poorer households spend a larger share of their budgets on food and energy and are thus more sensitive to price changes for these items.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: To investigate the disproportionate impact, two methods allow variation in the intensity of the shock faced by households (Kimura et al. 2026). In both cases, the average growth of the economy is maintained at the level indicated in Global Economic Prospects, June 2026 (World Bank 2026c), which captures the aggregate income and price shock. First, households are allocated sectoral growth rates based on their sector of employment. Second, inflation is allocated to households depending on their budget’s exposure to food and energy. Poorer households typically spend a greater share on food and energy and thus receive lower real income if the prices of these items rise. A distribution-neutral assumption, which is used as the baseline throughout the report, would instead assume the equal distribution of inflationary shocks.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: The baseline using projections of Global Economic Prospects, June 2026 (World Bank 2026c) provides estimates of the number of people living in extreme poverty at 811 million people in 2026 (refer to figure B1.2.1). This is an increase of 2.5 million people relative to the preconflict growth projections of Global Economic Prospects, January 2026 (World Bank 2026b). While these differences are not solely attributable to the conflict, the numbers confirm a worsening outlook.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: Allowing for distributional impacts either from uneven income shocks or price shocks leads to a further increase compared with the preconflict projections and essentially a stagnation in extreme poverty relative to 2025 (when the number was 816.9 million people). Taking the differential impact of sectoral growth rates into consideration reveals that 816.6 million people were estimated to be living in extreme poverty in 2026. One of the main reasons is that projected agricultural growth is much lower than the growth projected in the service and industrial sectors in 2026. Because a larger share of the extreme poor work in the agricultural sector, poverty reduction is muted because of the low agricultural growth. This also highlights that it is important for the poor to engage in resilient high-growth sectors to favor poverty reduction (refer to chapter 4).

text: BOX 1.2 Tracking the impact on poverty of the conflict in the Middle East (continued) The speed of extreme poverty reduction has shifted markedly over time. Between 1990 and 2004, the global rate of extreme poverty fell from 43 percent to 30 percent, with hundreds of millions of people pulled out of extreme poverty. As the fight against extreme poverty gained momentum in populous economies, most notably China, the global rate of extreme poverty fell starkly in the years after 2004, delivering substantial progress toward the goal of reducing extreme poverty across the globe. However, the momentum shifted in the late 2010s, even before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. The slowdown reflected persistently low economic growth in low-income economies leading to an increasing concentration of the global poor in these economies (World Bank 2018, 2024a). After a rise in the incidence of

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text:
extreme poverty in 2020, poverty rates began to decline, though at a slower pace than previously.

Had poverty continued to decline at the pace observed between 2000 and 2013, the extreme poverty rate would have reached roughly 7 percent by 2026, some 3 percentage points below the actual rate (refer to figure 1.1). In absolute terms, this gap represents approximately 240 million more people living in extreme poverty than would have been the case under the earlier trajectory of poverty reduction. The slowdown relative to the 2000–13 trend is only observable at the $3.00 line. At the higher poverty lines (for example, $4.20), actual poverty reduction has broadly kept pace with the pre-2013 trend.

text: BOX 1.3 The global middle class has grown, but economic security remains out of reach for many Living above the poverty line does not necessarily mean one has achieved middle-class status. A household that has escaped poverty may still face a substantial risk of falling back into poverty after an illness, a job loss, or a bad harvest, and this risk is what distinguishes the vulnerable from the middle class.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: In the approach developed by López-Calva and Ortiz-Juárez (2014), a household is middle class if the probability it will fall into poverty is low. The income level at which this probability becomes low is the economic security threshold, which marks the lower boundary of the middle class. Between the poor and the middle class lies a third group that is living above the poverty line, but does not enjoy sufficient security to have middle-class status. A large middle class is widely regarded as a foundation of stable growth because it helps sustain (continued)

text: 20 POVERTY , PROSPERITY , AND PLANET REPORT 2026 domestic demand, investment in education, and support for institutions that mediate distributional tensions (Banerjee and Duflo 2008; Easterly 2001). It is also a product of growth. As an economy’s average income rises, so does the share of the population that has attained economic security. The middle-income economies, home to about three-quarters of the world’s population (World Bank 2024b), are precisely the ones in which this transition is under way and far enough along that extreme poverty has receded, but not so far that security is the norm.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: The thresholds used in this report can serve as approximate class boundaries. Each of the three poverty lines is the typical national poverty line of an income group: $3.00 a day for low-income economies, $4.20 for lower-middle-income economies, and $8.30 for upper-middle-income economies (refer to box 1.1). Households living on less than $3.00 a day are extremely poor by any standard. Those living on between $3.00 and $8.30 are above the extreme poverty line, but would count as poor in a middle-income economy and, for the most part, remain short of economic security. Those living on between $8.30 and $28.00 a day are above the poverty line of every developing economy and constitute a global middle class; and those above $28.00 a day exceed the prosperity standard this report uses to gauge shared prosperity (refer to chapter 2). These thresholds are proxies. Ongoing work indicates that

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: the income required for security is higher than any poverty line.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: Applying the vulnerability approach to the World Bank’s harmonized household surveys—estimating, for each economy, the probability that a household is living on less than the poverty line of the relevant income group over a few years, and identifying the consumption level at which this probability becomes low—yields economic security lines of about $6.00, $7.00, and $14.00 a day for the three income groups. This is roughly twice the corresponding poverty lines, but with wide variation across economies (Bolch et al. 2026). The threshold also shifts with the risks households face. In Europe and Central Asia, the income needed to maintain a low probability of falling into poverty rose by about 10 percent in real terms between 2008 and 2018 as the shocks pushing households into poverty grew larger (Bussolo et al. 2025). There is no fixed income at which security begins. The boundary of the

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text:
middle class shifts with the environment in which households live.

Measured against these thresholds, the global middle class has grown substantially since 2000, roughly doubling as a share of the world’s population.

The group living on between $3.00 and $8.30 a day, however, has remained close to a third of the world’s population throughout the period. Among large numbers of people, the exit from extreme poverty has thus represented an exit into vulnerability rather than into security.

text: These patterns connect the report’s monitoring to the concerns of middle-income economies. More work and better-paying work help people escape poverty (refer to chapter 4). Stable, well-paid jobs also protect against falling back into poverty, and they therefore help households climb from vulnerability to security, an agenda that has particular force in locations where the vulnerable group is largest. Vulnerability to climate-related hazards—a distinct concept, reflecting the lack of the means to cope if a hazard strikes rather than the risk of falling back into poverty—extends well above the poverty line (refer to chapter 3). The $8.30 line and the $28.00 prosperity standard are precisely the boundaries within which the middle class is found.

text: 25 Global Poverty: Stalled Pro GreSS and riSinG Con Centration BOX 1.4 The Poverty and Inequality Platform has been updated with new data and revised regional classifications The data on poverty and inequality used throughout the report are available through the World Bank’s online tool for statistics on poverty, inequality, and shared prosperity: the Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP). The PIP data build primarily on national household surveys and are usually updated twice a year as national statistical offices around the world make new data available. The availability of recent survey data is crucial for the accuracy and reliability of the platform’s estimates of poverty and shared prosperity.

text: Any specific region is considered covered by data in a given year if the economies with at least one survey within a three-year window on either side of the year account for at least 50 percent of the region’s population. Because of a lack of data, neither the Middle East and North Africa nor Sub-Saharan Africa were included among the post-2020 data in Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2024 (World Bank 2024a). Since then, more recent data have become available for a number of populous economies, greatly increasing the regional and global coverage in the post-COVID years. The updates include data on Ethiopia (2021) and Nigeria (2022/23), which results in coverage for Sub-Saharan Africa up to 2024, as well as new data for the Arab Republic of Egypt (2021/22), India (2022/23, 2023/24), and Pakistan (2024/25).

As part of the September 2025 PIP update, new regional groupings were implemented to align with the revised World Bank regional groups. First, until then, some high-income economies had been excluded from the geographic regions, but included as a separate group referred to as Other High Income or Rest of the World.

Now, all high-income economies are included in the corresponding geographic regions, which means that a new region, North America, has been added. Second, the World Bank recently moved Afghanistan and Pakistan from the South Asia region to the Middle East and North Africa region, now labeled Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan (World Bank 2025d). text: 27 Global Poverty: Stalled Pro GreSS and riSinG Con Centration Welfare growth in MENAAP has shown a concerning pattern. Between 2000 and 2019, welfare grew modestly, at around 1.5 percent annually, across most of the distribution. However, welfare growth among the poorest percentiles has turned negative since 2020, even as incomes higher in the distribution have continued to grow modestly. This means that the poorest are not only failing to escape poverty, but are falling farther behind. Both insufficient growth and high levels of inequality limit how effectively growth translates into poverty reduction. Since 2010, per capita incomes in low-income economies have barely risen, averaging less than 0.1 percent growth annually (World Bank 2025a). The sustained growth accelerations that have historically driven large poverty reductions in low-income economies have largely disappeared (World

Global per capita income growth in low-income countries is projected to slow to its weakest pace since the COVID-19 pandemic, amid renewed energy-price shocks from the conflict in the Middle East (World Bank 2026c). Elsewhere, growth has remained stronger and more inclusive. South Asia, in particular, has shown strong, broad-based welfare gains across the distribution.4 Poverty is now concentrated in economies where progress has stopped Extreme poverty is highly concentrated geographically. More than half the extreme poor across the globe are concentrated in only 9 economies, and three-quarters are living in 20 economies (refer to figure 1.6).5 Of the nine economies, six are in Sub-Saharan Africa; the others are India, Pakistan, and the Republic of Y emen.

text: The countries with high populations of poor people are on the list because of large populations or because of high poverty rates, or both. For example, India is among the top nine economies by poor population not because of a high extreme poverty rate, but because it is the most populous country in the world. Whereas India’s extreme poverty rate has decreased substantially over the last 15 years, poverty rates have either stagnated or increased in the remaining eight economies. These statistics are subject to uncertainty, however. In some of these economies, such as Afghanistan and the Federal Republic of Somalia, no survey data exist, and poverty estimates must therefore be imputed (Mahler et al. 2026). In others, such as the Republic of Y emen, the last survey with relevant data is several years old, and estimates must be extrapolated forward.

Today’s low-income economies are also doing worse than they did in the past. The 26 economies classified as low-income economies today reduced extreme poverty at more than 2 percent annually during the 2000s, with average gross domestic product (GDP) per capita in each growing at a rate close to 3 percent (refer to figure 1.7). Progress has since slowed sharply.

Poverty reduction nearly stalled between 2010 and 2019, and, in the decade ending in 2024, extreme poverty in these economies rose, while GDP per capita declined. The progress of the 2000s has thus not been sustained.

text: This concentration means that the recent gains are fragile. Economic downturns, climate shocks, or conflict could push large numbers of people back into poverty, as the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated (Mahler et al. 2022).

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: After decades of progress, global extreme poverty is projected to rise That poverty is now concentrated in economies where progress has stalled has profound implications for the outlook on extreme poverty. Because the population is also growing most rapidly in these same economies, the rising share of the global population in these economies is pulling the global poverty rate upward, even if national rates do not worsen. The stalled reduction in poverty may not merely be a temporary setback.6 If per capita growth in these economies continues at the pace observed over 2015–24, the global extreme poverty rate and the number of people living in extreme poverty will increase by 2030 (refer to figure 1.9). This would represent an unprecedented reversal of the decades-long decline in the global number of the extreme poor.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: If these economies were to achieve the growth rates they experienced during 2000–09, the global poverty rate would still remain above 8 percent in 2030 even under these more optimistic assumptions. Current GDP forecasts show slower poverty reduction, resulting in a poverty rate above 9 percent in 2030. Only under sustained annual global GDP growth of 4 percent would the extreme poverty rate approach the ambitious 3 percent goal by 2050, two decades later than the initial target year. These simulations hold within-country inequality constant at today’s level. If economies manage to achieve pro-poor growth, the projected poverty rates would be lower.7 For example, growth in agriculture has been shown to benefit the poorest relatively more, although this effect dissipates as economies become richer (Beegle and Christiaensen 2019).

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

text: Poverty rates in many low-income economies, particularly those in a fragile and conflict- affected situation, are projected to decline only marginally.8 These same economies are projected to experience substantial population growth (refer to figure 1.10).9 Thus, it is the growing population in economies with high poverty rates, not the rising poverty rates, that give these economies greater weight in the aggregate poverty rate and that is driving the projections of rising global poverty rates. Fragile economies that are involved in conflict are at the center of this pattern. Economies such as the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Niger, Sudan, and the Federal Republic of Somalia combine some of the highest current poverty rates with some of the most rapid projected population growth.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: Educational attainment is strongly associated with poverty incidence. Individuals with no formal education in 2024 faced poverty rates of 22 percent, compared with only 6 percent among individuals with secondary education and 1 percent among individuals with tertiary education (refer to figure 1.13, panel b). Poverty declined by the greatest amount in absolute terms—12 percentage points—between 2013 and 2024 among individuals with no formal education. A Shapley decomposition of this decline reveals that, within economies, the poverty rate among individuals with no formal education fell by 15 percentage points (refer to annex 1B, figure 1B.3).13 This within-economy progress was highly concentrated. India alone accounted for roughly 70 percent of the progress, and five economies—Bangladesh, China, India, Indonesia, and Pakistan—accounted for nearly all the progress. The increase in the

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text:
concentration of the people with no schooling globally in higher-poverty regions slightly countered this reduction. In Sub-Saharan Africa, the region’s rising share of the global population with no schooling more than offset modest within-economy progress. The decline in poverty rates observed among individuals with no formal education would have been larger if not for this global shift toward Sub-Saharan Africa (which exhibits high poverty rates overall) in terms of the share of the global population with no schooling. A similar pattern holds in primary, secondary, and tertiary education. Thus, within-economy declines in poverty rates dominate, but are partly offset by compositional shifts across education levels.

The profile of poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa differs markedly from the profiles in other regions.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: Although poverty rates are substantially higher across all groups in Sub-Saharan Africa relative to the same groups in other regions, children under age 18 living in poor households account for more than half the extreme poor in MENAAP and Sub-Saharan Africa, compared with

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: 37 Global Poverty: Stalled Pro GreSS and riSinG Con Centration 30 percent to 46 percent in other regions. A decomposition of changing demographic profiles into geographic and within-region components reveals how these regional differences are reshaping the global profile (refer to annex 1B, figure 1B.4). The geographic concentration of poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa, which has a younger population structure relative to other regions, is entirely driving the rising share of children among people living in poor households globally. Within regions, the child share of the poor population has actually declined slightly.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: Globally, households with children face substantially higher poverty rates than households without children (De la Flor Giuffra et al. 2025), and the relevant trends diverged across different household types in 2013–24 (refer to figure 1.14, panel a). Poverty rates fell across all household types globally, but the pace varied. Declines were most rapid among two-adult households with children (18 percent to 12 percent) and among multiple-adult households with children (22 percent to 14 percent), as well as among households without children, which already had low rates. By contrast, declines were slower among households with one woman adult and children (24 percent to 21 percent). As a result, the gap in poverty rates between these household types and two-adult households with children widened over the decade, underscoring how the absence of a second working-age adult is an increasingly

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text:
important correlate of poverty.

These patterns should be interpreted with caution. Because poverty is measured on a per capita basis, household needs increase one-for-one with the number of household members, ignoring any household economies of scale that arise from resource-sharing within the household.

Jolliffe and Tetteh-Baah (2024) show that incorporating household economies of scale substantially changes the identification of who is poor and that the largest effects are in regions where the households are the largest.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: Trends in Sub-Saharan Africa differ slightly from the global pattern. There, households with children exhibit broadly similar poverty rates across household types, ranging from 46 percent to 50 percent in 2024, and barely changed over the preceding decade (refer to figure 1.14, panel b). The trends were mixed among households without children. Poverty among adult- only households was steady at near 14 percent, whereas rates among senior-only households without children fell from 21 percent to 16 percent.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: The conflict and fragility dimension reinforces the diverging progress. In non-FCS economies, poverty rates declined substantially between 2013 and 2024 across all household types (refer to figure 1.14, panel c). In FCS economies, by contrast, poverty rates rose among most household types with children (refer to figure 1.14, panel d). The increases were largest among households with one woman adult and children, in which poverty rose from 45 percent to 52 percent, and among multiple-adult households with children, from 43 to 51 percent. Households in which senior adults alone care for children also experienced a substantial rise, from 41 percent to 47 percent, whereas poverty in two-adult households with children was steady at 44 percent.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: In FCS economies, poverty among senior-only households without children, a category with few households, showed a substantive decline. As a result, household types with children in FCS economies now face poverty rates roughly four to seven times the rates in non-FCS economies.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: 39 Global Poverty: Stalled Pro GreSS and riSinG Con Centration Subnational disparities reveal persistent pockets of extreme poverty Although more people are now living in urban areas than in rural areas, poverty remains an overwhelmingly rural phenomenon (refer to figure 1.15). In 2024, 16 percent of rural residents were living in extreme poverty, compared with 5 percent of urban residents, a ratio of more than three to one. Both rates fell between 2013 and 2024, from 25 percent and 7 percent, respectively, but the gap remains wide. As a result, three-quarters of the global poor today reside in rural areas.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text: However, because of increasing urbanization, the share of poor people living in urban areas is expanding globally. In Sub-Saharan Africa, the share rose from 18 percent in 2013 to 26 percent in 2024, and elsewhere, from 22 percent to 28 percent. The urbanization of poverty reflects changes within regions—urbanization is advancing more quickly than the reduction of urban poverty—rather than the geographic shift of poverty toward Sub-Saharan Africa (refer to annex 1B, figure 1B.4, panel b).

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text:
This rural-urban disparity, however, is only the first layer of spatial concentration. Subnational poverty estimates reveal even sharper disparities within economies and regions (refer to figure 1.16 and annex 1B, figure 1B.5).14 In Sub-Saharan Africa, national averages mask enormous within-economy heterogeneity. In Nigeria, subregional rates range from 8 percent to 80 percent, and, in Kenya, from 5 percent to 85 percent, illustrating how much regions within an economy can differ. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, by contrast, poverty is pervasive.

Even the least-poor province has an extreme poverty rate of nearly 50 percent, and, in most provinces, the rate exceeds 90 percent.

text:
The East Asia and Pacific region and the Latin America and Caribbean region also display considerable within-region heterogeneity (refer to annex 1B, figure 1B.5). Although the median poverty rates there are modest (4 percent and 3 percent, respectively), both regions include subregions with rates comparable with those in Sub-Saharan Africa, about 60 percent or higher in parts of Haiti, the Solomon Islands, and Timor-Leste. South Asia exhibits a more compressed distribution. Poverty rates in most subregions are clustered below 10 percent. In Europe and Central Asia and in North America, rates are uniformly low. Medians are below 1 percent, and there are few outliers, except in Central Asia.

Subnational data reveal diverging trajectories that mirror global patterns of uneven progress.

The Kyrgyz Republic and the Philippines exemplify successful broad-based poverty reduction.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

text:
In the Kyrgyz Republic, nearly all regions experienced dramatic declines in poverty in 2015–23 (refer to map 1.1, panel a). Rates fell to single digits in regions that had previously shown poverty rates exceeding 40 percent, and several regions nearly eliminated extreme poverty.

The Philippines showed a similar pattern. Poverty rates declined throughout the country in

text:
41 Global Poverty: Stalled Pro GreSS and riSinG Con Centration 2015–23, though pockets of higher poverty persisted, especially in the south (refer to map 1.1, panel b).

Nigeria stands in contrast to these success stories (refer to map 1.1, panel c). Between 2018 and 2022, subnational poverty rates showed little improvement in the country. Though the gap was only four years, poverty rates worsened considerably in many states. The rates continued to climb in 2022 in the north, where poverty already exceeded 50 percent, and several states registered rates above 70 percent or 80 percent. This stagnation illustrates why Nigeria now hosts the largest population of the extreme poor globally.

metadata.section: Poverty persists unevenly across people and places

Guatemala also presents a more concerning picture of stagnation and reversal (refer to map 1.1, panel d). Between 2014 and 2023, the extreme poverty rate rose substantially in several departments, and only a handful achieved meaningful reductions. This mixed performance highlights that progress can stall even in middle-income economies.

text: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds Poverty can be described along other dimensions besides poverty thresholds set according to monetary measures of welfare relying on consumption or income. Deprivation can be defined by considering a cutoff determined using basic needs, and it can be defined in relative terms through a comparison among peers. Measurement along nonmonetary dimensions can be useful and revealing.

metadata.section: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds

text: The $3.00 international poverty line measures deprivation with respect to the most basic needs as defined across low-income economies. As an economy’s income level increases, the perception of the composition of these basic needs may evolve (Herforth et al. 2020; Jolliffe and Prydz 2016; World Bank 2024a). Measurement might shift to the application of relative poverty lines that establish the poverty threshold not only according to the requirements to satisfy basic needs, but typically relative to the average level of income or consumption.

metadata.section: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds

text: The societal poverty line, a relative measure of poverty, was developed to capture the shifting nature of deprivation across income levels. Following the recommendations of the Atkinson Commission on Global Poverty (World Bank 2017), the societal poverty line varies according to the living standards in an economy. It is set equal to $1.30, plus half the median consumption or income in the economy, with a floor at the $3.00 international poverty line (Foster et al. 2025) (refer to annex 1A). This (weakly) relative approach reflects a recognition that poverty partly involves exclusion from a normal life in a given society. It also allows the poverty line to be specific to an economy. Globally, the societal poverty line varies with average income in a way that approximately corresponds to the way national poverty lines vary with average income across countries (Foster et al. 2025; Jolliffe

metadata.section: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds

text:
and Prydz 2021).

Regional patterns in societal poverty, as measured by the societal poverty line, mirror the patterns observed in extreme poverty rates. Although the measure is only weakly relative (refer to figure 1.17, panel a), economies with high societal poverty lines tend to exhibit lower societal poverty rates. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for most economies with high societal poverty rates, consistent with the concentration of extreme poverty in the region (refer to figure 1.17, panel b). Higher-income economies typically exhibit lower societal poverty rates, despite their higher societal poverty lines. These comparisons depend on the level of inequality in an economy and, in particular, the concentration of people at the bottom tail (refer to chapter 2).

text: Multidimensional deprivations add depth to the poverty profile The World Bank’s absolute and societal poverty lines rely on the measurement of household monetary welfare through the level of consumption or income. The World Bank Multidimensional Poverty Measure (MPM), by contrast, incorporates measures of nonmonetary deprivation (World Bank 2026e). In addition to extreme poverty, which is measured in monetary terms, the MPM includes deprivations in education and access to basic infrastructure services (Lara Ibarra et al. 2026) (refer to annex 1A). (The components of the MPM are among the indicators discussed in chapters 3 and 4.) The MPM defines a household that is deprived along at least one of these three dimensions— monetary welfare, education, and access to infrastructure—as multidimensionally poor. Any person identified as poor using the international poverty line is also identified

metadata.section: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds

text: as poor using the MPM. In education, household deprivation is defined according to whether any children up to the age of grade 8 in the household is not enrolled in school or whether no adult in the household has completed primary education. In the case of infrastructure, household

metadata.section: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds

text:
45 Global Poverty: Stalled Pro GreSS and riSinG Con Centration deprivation is defined according to whether a household lacks access to one or more of the following: clean drinking water, sanitation, or electricity.

To calculate the measure, the MPM requires more data than the monetary poverty measure.

Data on the MPM are therefore available only for a smaller sample of economies. If economies with information available for any year after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic are considered (2020 or more recently), the MPM covered 103 economies as of September 2026.

Across these 103 economies, 16.7 percent have been identified as multidimensionally poor, compared with 11.3 percent using the international poverty line of $3.00-a-person-a-day (refer to table 1.1).

metadata.section: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds

text: Extreme poverty rates generally coincide with deprivations in other dimensions (World Bank 2026e) (refer to figure 1.18). There may be wide variations, however, whereby economies associated with high monetary extreme poverty rates nonetheless exhibit low rates of nonmonetary deprivation.
